course.title: Azure Fundamentals Capstone
course.description: Build a small company in Azure in four weeks: a network, a VM, a website with HTTPS and a serverless counter — then watch it run.
course.audience: Four roles build a real Azure environment in four weeks, on a $5 budget. Start here.

roles.name: Cloud Architect
roles.mission: Owns the design, the standards, the cost and each week’s document.
roles.label: 📐 Cloud Architect

roles.name: Infrastructure Admin
roles.mission: Builds the network, the VM, the data and the templates.
roles.label: 🧱 Infrastructure Admin

roles.name: App & DevOps
roles.mission: Ships the website, the API and the pipeline.
roles.label: 🚀 App & DevOps

roles.name: Security & Ops
roles.mission: Locks access down, watches it run, and works the incidents.
roles.label: 🛡️ Security & Ops

weeks.objective: Set the standard and the $5 budget, then lay the network everything else sits in.
weeks.milestone: A budget alerts at $4, the resource group and VNet exist with the agreed names and tags, and the team repo is live.

Create the resource group and VNet

weeks.objective: Publish the company website over HTTPS and bring up one small Linux VM, reachable only from you.
weeks.milestone: The site loads over HTTPS, the B1s VM runs in snet-app, SSH works from your IP only, and the VM is deallocated.

Allow SSH from your IP only

Work one incident layer by layer

tasks.title: Set the naming standard and the budget
tasks.objective: Agree how everything is named and tagged, and cap spending at $5 before anything is built.
definitionOfDone: The naming and tag table is agreed

steps.title: Create the $5 budget
steps.description: The budget budget-capstone-team01 is listed with a $5 amount and one alert at 80%.
steps.instruction: Create a $5 monthly budget that emails the team.
instructionList: Search Cost Management → Budgets → Add.
Scope: your subscription. Name: budget-capstone-team01. Amount: 5.
Alert condition: Actual, 80%. Recipient: the team email.
Create.
steps.expectedOutput: The budget budget-capstone-team01 is listed with a $5 amount and one alert at 80%.
steps.whatItMeans: The budget is the guardrail. It is created first because it is the one thing that tells you a mistake is costing money.

fixes.fix: Student subscriptions sometimes need the Billing Reader role — ask the instructor, or set the budget at resource-group scope.

steps.title: Agree the naming and tags
steps.description: A table of prefixes and four tag keys everyone has agreed to use.
steps.instruction: Agree one naming pattern and four tags as a team.
instructionList: Pattern: type prefix, workload, team — e.g. vm-tools-team01.
Use the Azure abbreviations: rg-, vnet-, snet-, nsg-, vm-, st, func-, kv-.
Tags: project, team, env, owner.
steps.expectedOutput: A table of prefixes and four tag keys everyone has agreed to use.
steps.whatItMeans: A name you can read tells you the type, the purpose and the owner without opening anything. Week 11 enforces the owner tag.

steps.title: Record it in the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard
steps.description: Your section: Account and guardrails, Naming, Tags, RACI.
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard.
instructionList: Subscription, region (eastus) and the budget.
One naming row per resource type you will create.
The four tags, and a short RACI.
steps.whatItMeans: This is the standard every later document and template refers to.

tasks.title: Create the resource group and VNet
tasks.objective: Create the resource group and a virtual network with its first subnet, named and tagged by the standard.

steps.title: Create the resource group
steps.instruction: Create the tagged resource group in eastus.

commands.cmd: az group create -n rg-capstone-team01 -l eastus --tags project=capstone team=team01 env=dev owner=team01-infra
commands.explain: A resource group is the folder every resource lives in; deleting it deletes them all.

steps.whatItMeans: Everything this course builds lives in this one group, so cost, access and clean-up happen in one place.

steps.title: Create the VNet and first subnet
steps.description: Create the VNet and first subnet
steps.instruction: Create the VNet 10.10.0.0/16 with snet-app 10.10.1.0/24.

commands.cmd: az network vnet create -g rg-capstone-team01 -n vnet-capstone-team01 --address-prefix 10.10.0.0/16 --subnet-name snet-app --subnet-prefix 10.10.1.0/24
commands.explain: The VNet is your private network; the subnet is the slice the VM will use.

steps.whatItMeans: A /16 leaves room for 256 /24 subnets; the course uses two. Private ranges (RFC 1918) never route on the internet.

fixes.fix: Run the previous step first, and check the name is exactly rg-capstone-team01.

steps.title: Record it in the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard.
instructionList: The resource group and VNet names.
The address space and the first subnet.
steps.whatItMeans: The Network Design Document in Week 6 starts from these numbers.

tasks.title: Open the team repository and board
tasks.objective: Create the team repository, a README with the naming standard, and a twelve-week board.
definitionOfDone: The repo exists with a README
The board has this week’s four tasks

steps.title: Create the repository
steps.description: A private repository with a README and four folders, shared with the team.
steps.instruction: Create the team repository with a README.
instructionList: New repository: capstone-team01, private, add a README.
Invite your three teammates as collaborators.
Folders: site/, api/, infra/, docs/.
steps.expectedOutput: A private repository with a README and four folders, shared with the team.
steps.whatItMeans: Everything the team produces lives here — the site, the function, the template and the documents.

steps.title: Create the board
steps.description: A board with four assigned cards, linked from the README.
steps.instruction: Create a board with this week’s four tasks.
instructionList: New project (Board). Columns: To do, Doing, Done.
Add one card per role for Week 1 and assign it.
Link the board from the README.
steps.expectedOutput: A board with four assigned cards, linked from the README.
steps.whatItMeans: A board makes the four independent tasks visible, so nobody waits on anybody without knowing it.

steps.title: Record it in the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard.
instructionList: The repository URL.
The board URL.
steps.whatItMeans: The handover package in Week 12 points a new team at this repository.

tasks.title: Put an NSG on the subnet
tasks.objective: Create a network security group, attach it to snet-app, and review who has access to the subscription.

steps.title: Create and attach the NSG
steps.instruction: Create the NSG and attach it to snet-app.

commands.cmd: az network nsg create -g rg-capstone-team01 -n nsg-snet-app-team01
commands.explain: An NSG is a stateful firewall. It starts with default rules that deny all inbound from the internet.

commands.cmd: az network vnet subnet update -g rg-capstone-team01 --vnet-name vnet-capstone-team01 -n snet-app --nsg nsg-snet-app-team01
commands.explain: Attaching it to the subnet protects everything placed there, including the VM next week.

steps.whatItMeans: Attach at the subnet, not the VM, so a resource added later is protected from its first second.

steps.title: Read the default rules
steps.instruction: List the NSG’s default rules.

commands.cmd: az network nsg rule list -g rg-capstone-team01 --nsg-name nsg-snet-app-team01 --include-default -o table
commands.explain: Shows the built-in rules. The last inbound rule, DenyAllInBound, is why nothing reaches the VM until you allow it.
commands.sample:
Name                 Priority  Access  Direction
AllowVnetInBound     65000     Allow   Inbound
DenyAllInBound       65500     Deny    Inbound

steps.whatItMeans: Knowing the defaults is how you know every Allow you add is a decision.

steps.title: Review access (RBAC)
steps.description: A list of role assignments on the subscription.
steps.instruction: List who holds which role on the subscription.
instructionList: Subscription → Access control (IAM) → Role assignments.
Note each person or group, their role and scope.
steps.expectedOutput: A list of role assignments on the subscription.
steps.whatItMeans: Least privilege starts with knowing what is granted today. Week 5 narrows it.

steps.title: Record it in the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard.
instructionList: One row per person or group and what they get.
steps.whatItMeans: The Week 5 access matrix builds on this list.

tasks.title: Write the architecture document and cost
tasks.objective: Estimate the monthly cost of each component, then record the first architecture decision with what was rejected.
definitionOfDone: Every component has a monthly cost

steps.title: Price it
steps.description: A monthly estimate per service, with the VM the largest line.
steps.instruction: Price the components in the Azure pricing calculator.
instructionList: Add: Virtual Machines (B1s, Linux, 730 h), Storage Accounts (LRS, 1 GB).
Add: Functions (Consumption), Azure Cosmos DB (serverless).
Read the monthly total; then halve the VM hours — you deallocate it.
steps.expectedOutput: A monthly estimate per service, with the VM the largest line.
steps.whatItMeans: Cost is an architecture property. Knowing which line dominates tells you what to switch off.

steps.title: Write ADR-001
steps.description: ADR-001 with context, decision, rejected options and consequences.
steps.instruction: Record why the site is a storage static website.
instructionList: Context: a public site with HTTPS for under $1 a month.
Decision: storage static website — HTTPS is built in.
Rejected: a VM with nginx, and Front Door (about $35 a month).
steps.expectedOutput: ADR-001 with context, decision, rejected options and consequences.
steps.whatItMeans: An ADR records the decision and the alternatives, so the next team does not reopen it without new facts.

steps.title: Record it in the Solution Architecture Document
steps.description: Your section: Components and cost, ADR-001.
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Solution Architecture Document.
instructionList: One component per row, with its monthly cost.
steps.whatItMeans: The architecture document grows every week and is handed over in Week 12.

tasks.title: Deploy the tools VM
tasks.objective: Deploy a B1s Ubuntu VM into snet-app with SSH-key sign-in only, then deallocate it.
definitionOfDone: The VM is deallocated at the end

steps.title: Create the VM
steps.instruction: Create the B1s VM in snet-app, SSH key only.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; VM=vm-tools-team01; az vm create -g $RG -n $VM --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_B1s --vnet-name vnet-capstone-team01 --subnet snet-app --nsg "" --public-ip-sku Standard --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys --tags project=capstone team=team01 env=dev owner=team01-infra
commands.explain: --nsg "" skips a per-VM NSG: the subnet’s NSG already protects it. --generate-ssh-keys means no password exists to guess.

steps.whatItMeans: B1s is the free-tier size. Key-only sign-in removes password guessing entirely.

fixes.fix: B1s is out of capacity in that region. Try eastus2 for the VM only, and record why.
Student subscriptions allow few vCPUs. Delete any other VM first.

steps.title: Read its network facts
steps.instruction: Read the VM’s private IP and NIC.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; VM=vm-tools-team01; az vm list-ip-addresses -g $RG -n $VM -o table
commands.explain: The private IP is what other resources use; the public IP only exists for outbound patching.

steps.whatItMeans: The private IP comes from snet-app — 10.10.1.4 because Azure reserves the first four addresses.

steps.title: Record it in the Solution Architecture Document
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Solution Architecture Document.
instructionList: Name, size, private IP, operating system.
steps.whatItMeans: The runbook in Week 7 and the snapshot in Week 8 start from these facts.

steps.title: Deallocate the VM
steps.instruction: Stop the VM so it stops costing money.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; VM=vm-tools-team01; az vm deallocate -g $RG -n $VM
commands.explain: Deallocate releases the compute. A VM that is only "stopped" from inside still bills.
commands.sample: (no output — returns when the VM is deallocated)

commands.cmd: az vm get-instance-view -g $RG -n $VM --query "instanceView.statuses[1].displayStatus" -o tsv
commands.explain: Reads the power state back.

steps.whatItMeans: A running B1s costs about 1 cent an hour; a forgotten one eats the budget in weeks.

tasks.title: Publish the website with HTTPS
tasks.objective: Publish the company website from a storage account static website, HTTPS-only, then change it and redeploy.

steps.title: Create the storage account
steps.instruction: Create an HTTPS-only storage account with TLS 1.2.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; WEB=stwebteam01$RANDOM; echo $WEB
commands.explain: Storage names are global, 3–24 lowercase letters and digits. $RANDOM makes yours unique; write it down.

commands.cmd: az storage account create -g $RG -n $WEB --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 --https-only true --min-tls-version TLS1_2 --allow-blob-public-access false
commands.explain: HTTPS-only and TLS 1.2 refuse old, insecure connections. Blob public access stays off; the website endpoint still serves.

steps.whatItMeans: The static-website endpoint serves HTTPS with Microsoft’s certificate, so no CDN is needed.

steps.title: Enable the website and upload
steps.instruction: Switch on the static website and upload index.html.

commands.cmd: az storage blob service-properties update --account-name $WEB --static-website --index-document index.html --404-document 404.html --auth-mode login
commands.explain: Creates the $web container and serves it as a website.

commands.cmd: az storage blob upload-batch --account-name $WEB -s ./site -d '$web' --auth-mode login --overwrite
commands.explain: Uploads the site folder. You need the Storage Blob Data Contributor role for --auth-mode login.

commands.cmd: az storage account show -n $WEB --query primaryEndpoints.web -o tsv
commands.explain: Prints the site’s address.

steps.whatItMeans: Upload again after any change — that is a redeploy. Week 10 automates it.

fixes.fix: Assign yourself Storage Blob Data Contributor on the account, wait a minute, retry.

steps.title: Record it in the Solution Architecture Document
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Solution Architecture Document.
instructionList: The HTTPS URL.
How you redeployed a change.
steps.whatItMeans: The site URL is the origin CORS will admit in Week 3.

tasks.title: Allow SSH from your IP only
tasks.objective: Add one inbound rule allowing SSH from your own address, then prove it is allowed from you and blocked elsewhere.
definitionOfDone: SSH is blocked from Cloud Shell

steps.title: Add the SSH rule
steps.instruction: Allow TCP 22 from your IP address only.

commands.cmd: MYIP=$(curl -s https://ifconfig.me); echo $MYIP
commands.explain: Run this on YOUR laptop, not Cloud Shell: it prints the address your laptop reaches the internet from.

commands.cmd: az network nsg rule create -g rg-capstone-team01 --nsg-name nsg-snet-app-team01 -n Allow-SSH-MyIP --priority 1000 --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp --source-address-prefixes $MYIP/32 --destination-port-ranges 22
commands.explain: A /32 is exactly one address. Priority 1000 is evaluated before the default deny at 65500.

steps.whatItMeans: Never 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22: bots scan the whole internet for open SSH within minutes.

steps.title: Test allowed and blocked
steps.description: SSH connects from your laptop and times out from Cloud Shell.
steps.instruction: Test SSH from your laptop, then from Cloud Shell.
instructionList: Start the VM: az vm start -g rg-capstone-team01 -n vm-tools-team01.
From your laptop: ssh azureuser@PUBLIC_IP — expect a prompt.
From Cloud Shell: the same command — expect a timeout.
Deallocate the VM when done.
steps.expectedOutput: SSH connects from your laptop and times out from Cloud Shell.
steps.whatItMeans: A rule is only proved when something that should fail does fail.

fixes.fix: Your IP changed (Wi-Fi, VPN). Re-run the first command and update the rule.

steps.title: Record it in the Solution Architecture Document
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Solution Architecture Document.
instructionList: One allowed row, one blocked row.
steps.whatItMeans: Week 6 removes this rule entirely; this record is the before.

tasks.title: Draw the request flow with real URLs
tasks.objective: Trace how a page view becomes a count in the database, naming every real URL and resource.

steps.title: Read Architecture v3
steps.description: You can name every hop from the browser to the database.
steps.instruction: Open the architecture diagram at week 3.
instructionList: Move the slider to v3. New resources glow.
Follow the solid arrows from Visitors to Cosmos DB.
Click the Function App: the template highlights its lines.
steps.expectedOutput: You can name every hop from the browser to the database.
steps.whatItMeans: The diagram is drawn from the template, so it is the environment you are building, not an illustration.

steps.title: Write the flow
steps.description: A three-hop flow with real URLs and resource names.
steps.instruction: Write the flow with your real URLs.
instructionList: Browser → https://your-site (storage static website).
Page script → GET https://func-…/api/visitorCount.
Function → Cosmos DB database capstone, container visitors, item id "site".
steps.expectedOutput: A three-hop flow with real URLs and resource names.
steps.whatItMeans: A flow with real URLs is testable. Week 6 tests each hop.

steps.title: Record it in the Application & API Design Specification
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Application & API Design Specification.
instructionList: The flow, hop by hop.
steps.whatItMeans: Week 6’s path tests follow this flow.

tasks.title: Create Cosmos DB and seed the counter
tasks.objective: Create a serverless Cosmos DB account, a database and a container, and seed the counter item.

steps.title: Create the account
steps.instruction: Create a serverless Cosmos DB account.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; COSMOS=cosmos-capstone-team01-$RANDOM; az cosmosdb create -g $RG -n $COSMOS --capabilities EnableServerless --default-consistency-level Session
commands.explain: Serverless bills per request, so an idle counter costs nearly nothing. This takes a few minutes.

steps.whatItMeans: Provisioned throughput would charge every hour even when nobody visits.

steps.title: Create the database and container
steps.instruction: Create database capstone and container visitors.

commands.cmd: az cosmosdb sql database create -g $RG -a $COSMOS -n capstone
commands.explain: A database groups containers.

commands.cmd: az cosmosdb sql container create -g $RG -a $COSMOS -d capstone -n visitors --partition-key-path /id
commands.explain: The partition key decides how data is spread. /id suits one small item.

steps.whatItMeans: Choosing the partition key is the one Cosmos DB decision you cannot change later.

steps.title: Seed the counter item
steps.description: The item "site" with count 0 is listed.
steps.where: Azure portal — Cosmos DB → Data Explorer
steps.instruction: Add the item { "id": "site", "count": 0 }.
instructionList: capstone → visitors → Items → New item.
Replace the body with { "id": "site", "count": 0 } and Save.
steps.expectedOutput: The item "site" with count 0 is listed.
steps.whatItMeans: The Function reads and updates this one item.

steps.title: Record it in the Application & API Design Specification
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Application & API Design Specification.
instructionList: Account, database, container.
Partition key and the seed item.
steps.whatItMeans: The API spec’s data model.

tasks.title: Build the visitor-counter Function
tasks.objective: Create a Function App with an HTTP trigger that increments the counter, and show the count on the site.
learn: Calling an API from a page

steps.title: Create the Function App
steps.instruction: Create a Consumption Function App for Node.js.
instructionList: Resource group rg-capstone-team01. Name func-capstone-team01-XXXX.
Runtime Node.js 20, Windows, Consumption plan.
Monitoring: enable Application Insights. Create.
steps.whatItMeans: Windows Consumption is the plan that lets you edit code in the portal, and it costs nothing at this scale.

steps.title: Add the counter function
steps.description: The function is listed and its Get function URL works.
steps.instruction: Add an HTTP function with Cosmos DB bindings.
instructionList: HTTP trigger, name visitorCount, authorization Anonymous.
Integration: input and output binding to Cosmos DB, database capstone, container visitors, id site.
Code: read count, add 1, write it back, return { count }.
steps.expectedOutput: The function is listed and its Get function URL works.
steps.whatItMeans: Bindings do the database calls, so the code is four lines. The read-then-write is a known race — fine for a counter.

fixes.fix: Choose New → your Cosmos DB account. The portal stores a connection setting; Week 5 replaces it with the identity.

steps.title: Call it and show it
steps.instruction: Call the API, then add the count to the page.

commands.cmd: FUNC=https://func-capstone-team01-XXXX.azurewebsites.net; curl -s $FUNC/api/visitorCount
commands.explain: Each call adds one. Then add fetch() of this URL to site/index.html, writing the result into #visitor-count, and upload again.

steps.whatItMeans: The page calls the API from the browser, which is why CORS matters next.

steps.title: Record it in the Application & API Design Specification
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Application & API Design Specification.
instructionList: GET /api/visitorCount, what it returns, its status codes.
steps.whatItMeans: The spec another developer would call your API from.

tasks.title: Lock CORS and keep secrets out
tasks.objective: Allow only your site to call the API from a browser, prove another origin is refused, and keep keys out of the page.

steps.title: Allow only your site
steps.instruction: Set CORS to your site origin only.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; FN=func-capstone-team01-XXXX; SITE=https://stwebteam0118342.z13.web.core.windows.net
commands.explain: Set these to your own names. The origin has no trailing slash.

commands.cmd: az functionapp cors add -g $RG -n $FN --allowed-origins $SITE && az functionapp cors show -g $RG -n $FN
commands.explain: Browsers only let pages from listed origins read the API’s answers.

steps.whatItMeans: Remove "*" if the portal added it. A wildcard lets any website use your API from its visitors’ browsers.

steps.title: Prove a foreign origin is refused
steps.description: Prove a foreign origin is refused
steps.instruction: Call the API as another website would.

commands.cmd: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "Origin: https://evil.example" https://$FN.azurewebsites.net/api/visitorCount | grep -i access-control || echo "no CORS header — refused"
commands.explain: A foreign origin gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, so its browser discards the answer.

steps.whatItMeans: CORS protects browsers, not the API: curl still gets a count. That is why the API holds no secrets.

steps.title: Keep secrets out of the page
steps.description: No key in the page; the Cosmos setting points at Key Vault.
steps.where: Browser DevTools, then the Function App
steps.instruction: Check the page and settings hold no key.
instructionList: View the site source: only the API URL, no key.
Function App → Environment variables: the Cosmos setting should be a Key Vault reference, not a raw key.
steps.expectedOutput: No key in the page; the Cosmos setting points at Key Vault.
steps.whatItMeans: Anything in page source is public. Week 5 removes the key altogether.

steps.title: Record it in the Application & API Design Specification
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Application & API Design Specification.
instructionList: The allowed origin, the negative test, where the credential lives.
steps.whatItMeans: The first line of the secrets register.

tasks.title: Report the cost to date

steps.title: Read the cost
steps.description: A per-service cost for the month so far.
steps.where: Azure portal — Cost Management → Cost analysis
steps.instruction: Group cost by service for this month.
instructionList: Scope: rg-capstone-team01. View: Accumulated costs.

Compare with your Week 2 estimate.
steps.expectedOutput: A per-service cost for the month so far.
steps.whatItMeans: Actual cost against the estimate is how you find what you forgot to switch off.

steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Monitoring & Incident Report.

steps.whatItMeans: Week 11 turns this into the cost report.

tasks.title: Alert on Function errors
tasks.objective: Create an action group and an alert that emails when the Function returns server errors.
definitionOfDone: The alert exists and emails the team

steps.title: Create the action group
steps.instruction: Create an action group that emails the team.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; az monitor action-group create -g $RG -n ag-capstone-team01 --short-name capstone --action email team team01-alerts@school.edu
commands.explain: An action group is who gets told and how. Alerts point at it.

steps.whatItMeans: One action group, many alerts: change the email once.

steps.title: Create the alert
steps.instruction: Alert when Http5xx is above zero in five minutes.

commands.cmd: FNID=$(az functionapp show -g $RG -n func-capstone-team01-XXXX --query id -o tsv); az monitor metrics alert create -g $RG -n alert-func-5xx-team01 --scopes $FNID --condition "total Http5xx > 0" --window-size 5m --evaluation-frequency 1m --action ag-capstone-team01
commands.explain: Http5xx counts server errors. Any error in five minutes fires the alert.

steps.whatItMeans: Errors are the signal users feel. CPU on a serverless app tells you little.

steps.title: Record it in the Monitoring & Incident Report
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Monitoring & Incident Report.
instructionList: The signal, where it is measured, the threshold, the action.
steps.whatItMeans: The monitoring half of the incident report.

tasks.title: Find a failure in Application Insights
tasks.objective: Break the API on purpose, find the exception in Application Insights, and restore it.

steps.title: Break it
steps.description: The counter shows no number; the API returns 500.
steps.instruction: Rename the Cosmos setting so the Function fails.
instructionList: Copy the Cosmos connection setting’s name somewhere safe.
Rename it by adding _OFF. Apply.
Load the site twice: the counter fails.
steps.expectedOutput: The counter shows no number; the API returns 500.
steps.whatItMeans: Breaking it yourself means you know the answer, so you can learn the tool that finds it.

steps.title: Find it
steps.description: An exception naming the missing Cosmos setting.
steps.instruction: Find the exception in Application Insights.
instructionList: Operations tab: visitorCount shows failed requests.
Open a sample: the exception names the missing setting.
steps.expectedOutput: An exception naming the missing Cosmos setting.
steps.whatItMeans: The exception names the layer — configuration — before you open any code.

steps.title: Restore it
steps.description: The counter shows a number again.
steps.instruction: Rename the setting back and retest.
instructionList: Remove _OFF, Apply, reload the site.
steps.expectedOutput: The counter shows a number again.
steps.whatItMeans: A fix is not done until the retest passes.

steps.title: Record it in the Monitoring & Incident Report
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Monitoring & Incident Report.
instructionList: Add a signal row for exceptions in Application Insights.
steps.whatItMeans: Your half of the monitoring table.

tasks.title: Work one incident layer by layer
tasks.objective: Break CORS on purpose, then work it as an incident: symptom, layer, evidence, root cause, fix, prevention.
definitionOfDone: An incident record with all six parts

steps.title: Inject the fault
steps.instruction: Remove your site from CORS.

commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01; FN=func-capstone-team01-XXXX; SITE=https://stwebteam0118342.z13.web.core.windows.net; az functionapp cors remove -g $RG -n $FN --allowed-origins $SITE
commands.explain: The page will still load, but its script can no longer read the count.

steps.whatItMeans: A realistic fault: nothing is “down”, one feature silently stops.

steps.title: Find the layer
steps.description: The console names CORS as the cause.
steps.instruction: Follow the symptom down the layers.
instructionList: Symptom: the count is missing.
Network tab: the API returned 200 — the network and app layers work.
Console: “blocked by CORS policy” — the configuration layer.
steps.expectedOutput: The console names CORS as the cause.
steps.whatItMeans: Working down the layers stops you fixing what is not broken.

steps.title: Fix and retest
steps.instruction: Add the origin back and reload.

commands.cmd: az functionapp cors add -g $RG -n $FN --allowed-origins $SITE
commands.explain: Restores the rule. Reload the site: the count returns.

steps.whatItMeans: Week 10 puts CORS in the template, so drift like this is corrected by the next deploy.

steps.title: Record it in the Monitoring & Incident Report
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Monitoring & Incident Report.
instructionList: Symptom, layer, evidence, root cause, fix, prevention.
steps.whatItMeans: Week 12 runs this loop again under time pressure.

deliverables.standard: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework — naming and tagging
deliverables.purpose: The rules every later resource obeys: where it lives in Azure, what it is called, how it is tagged, who does what, and the spending limit that stops a mistake costing money.
deliverables.howTo: Each role fills its own section. Agree the naming pattern first — everything built later is named from it.
buildSteps: Architect: agree the naming pattern and tags, set the $5 budget, draw Architecture v1.
Infrastructure: create the resource group and VNet; record their real names and address space.
App / DevOps: create the team repository and board; link them.
Security & Ops: record the NSG rules and who has which access.
deliverables.meaning: A good standard lets a stranger read any resource name and know what it is, whose it is and which environment it belongs to.
deliverables.useIt: Every week reads it. The Week 11 policy enforces its tags automatically.
pitfalls: Names that differ from the pattern — the policy in Week 11 will flag them.
A budget with no email address — it alerts nobody.

commands.label: Pick the resource group
commands.cmd: RG=rg-capstone-team01

commands.label: Check the template before anything changes
commands.cmd: az deployment group validate -g $RG --template-file azuredeploy.json --parameters @azuredeploy.parameters.dev.json

commands.label: Preview exactly what will change
commands.cmd: az deployment group what-if -g $RG --template-file azuredeploy.json --parameters @azuredeploy.parameters.dev.json

commands.label: Deploy
commands.cmd: az deployment group create -g $RG --template-file azuredeploy.json --parameters @azuredeploy.parameters.dev.json

commands.label: Switch on the static website (ARM cannot)
commands.cmd: az storage blob service-properties update --account-name $WEB --static-website --index-document index.html --404-document 404.html --auth-mode login

notes: ARM cannot switch on the static-website feature — it is a data-plane setting. One CLI command does it after the deployment.
The Function’s code is not in the template. It ships through the portal in Week 3 and through GitHub Actions from Week 10.
Secret values never live in a template. The vault is created here; you add secrets to it, and the Function reads them with its identity.
Deploy with throughWeek=4 or 8 to get the environment exactly as the Fundamentals or the Administrator course leaves it; every later resource is conditional on it.
The VM keeps a public IP only so it can download patches. Production would use a NAT gateway; this course avoids its monthly cost and opens no inbound port instead.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).

glossary.data.src_ip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a network (Suricata) alert — who the traffic came from.
glossary.data.srcip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a host alert (logins, web requests). Its network twin is data.src_ip — search both.
glossary.ossec.conf: The Wazuh agent's config file. It names the SOC to report to and any extra log files to ship.
glossary.hydra: A password-guessing tool. In this lab you run it against your own pod so the SOC has a brute-force attack to detect.
glossary.tcpdump: A command-line tool that records network traffic to a .pcap file you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.Wireshark: A traffic viewer. Open a .pcap in it and "Follow HTTP Stream" to read the exact request an attacker sent.
glossary.Kali: The attacker machine in your lab — a Linux build that ships with nmap, nikto, hydra and the rest.
glossary.Proxmox: A hypervisor — an operating system whose job is to run virtual machines. In Server+ you install it on your own server; in the CySA lab it already runs the lab.
glossary.POST: Power-On Self-Test — the hardware check a machine runs the moment you power it on, before any operating system. Beeps and blink codes are POST talking to you.
glossary.DIMM: A memory stick. Which slots they go in is dictated by the motherboard manual, and the wrong slots can stop the machine starting at all.
glossary.ECC: Error-Correcting Code memory — server RAM that detects and fixes single-bit corruption on the fly. Servers use it; desktops usually do not.
glossary.HCL: Hardware Compatibility List — the check that the software you plan to run officially supports the exact hardware you have, before you build on it.
glossary.UEFI: The modern replacement for the old BIOS firmware. Boot mode matters: an OS installed under UEFI will not boot if the firmware is later switched to legacy.
glossary.IOMMU: The chip feature (Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi) that lets a virtual machine be handed a real piece of hardware, like a NIC, as its own.
glossary.VT-x: Intel’s virtualization extensions. Present is not enough — they must be ENABLED in firmware setup, or the hypervisor cannot start a single VM.
glossary.stripe size: How large a chunk of data a RAID array writes to one disk before moving to the next. The default is right for this build.
glossary.IDS: Intrusion Detection System — software that watches traffic and raises an alert when it matches a known attack pattern. Suricata is yours.
glossary.NVD: National Vulnerability Database — the public catalogue you search to find a CVE and its score for a given software version.
glossary.pod: Your team’s pair of machines: one Ubuntu web server and one Windows PC.
glossary.escalate: Pass an alert on for deeper investigation, with the reason written down, instead of closing it yourself.
glossary.SOC: Security Operations Centre — the team (and dashboard) that watches for attacks around the clock.
glossary.SIEM: Security Information and Event Management — software that gathers logs from everywhere and raises alerts. Wazuh is your SIEM.
glossary.IOC: Indicator of Compromise — a clue an attacker leaves behind, like a bad IP address, file name, or hash.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public ID for one specific known software flaw, e.g. CVE-2021-41773.
glossary.CVSS: A 0–10 score for how severe a vulnerability is, so you can rank what to fix first.
glossary.pcap: A 'packet capture' — a saved recording of network traffic you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.SQLi: SQL injection — tricking a website into running database commands it shouldn't, often to steal data.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall — a filter in front of a website that blocks common attacks like SQL injection.
glossary.POA&M: Plan of Action & Milestones — a to-do list for fixing findings: what, who owns it, and by when.
glossary.PTES: Penetration Testing Execution Standard — the agreed steps of a pentest: recon, scan, exploit, report.
glossary.STRIDE: A checklist of threat types: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
glossary.NIC: Network Interface Card — a machine's network connection. On these VMs it's usually named ens18.
glossary.IaC: Infrastructure as Code — describing machines in a text file a tool applies, so the build is repeatable and the file is the record. Terraform or OpenTofu is yours.
glossary.OpenTofu: The open-source fork of Terraform, kept under the Linux Foundation after HashiCorp changed Terraform’s licence in 2023. Same HCL, same providers, same state files; the command is tofu instead of terraform.
glossary.exporter: A small program on a host that publishes its metrics on an HTTP port for Prometheus to collect. node_exporter for Linux, windows_exporter for Windows.
glossary.IPAM: IP Address Management — the tool that holds every subnet and address and who has it, so the plan and reality are the same document. NetBox is yours.
glossary.FIM: File Integrity Monitoring — an agent that hashes important files and alerts when one changes, which is how a tampered config gets noticed.
glossary.cloud-init: The first-boot setup a cloud image runs: hostname, user, keys and addressing handed in from outside, so a clone comes up configured instead of blank.
glossary.DNAT: Destination NAT — the host rewriting where a packet is going. The rule that turns a request to the host’s campus address on port 80 into a request to websrv in the DMZ.
glossary.MASQUERADE: Source NAT behind the host’s own address, so a reply from the campus LAN or the internet comes back to the host and is handed to the guest that asked.
glossary.published port: A port on the host’s campus address that a DNAT rule hands to a VM behind it. Each one is a deliberate hole in the segmentation, and you should be able to say why it exists.
glossary.idempotent: Running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The property that makes a playbook safe to run every night — and why changed=0 on the second run is the proof.
glossary.drift: Reality diverging from what the code says — a change made in the console instead of the repository. terraform plan (tofu plan) detects it; the next apply may undo it.
glossary.dynamic inventory: Ansible asking the hypervisor which hosts exist instead of reading a list someone typed. The list is never out of date because there is no list.
glossary.XDR: Extended Detection and Response — one platform watching endpoints, logs and files across a whole fleet. Wazuh on the Core is the MSP’s.
glossary.verify job: The backup server re-reading a backup, chunk by chunk, to confirm it is restorable before anyone needs it.
glossary.SLO: Service Level Objective — the availability you promise a client, as a number. The SLA is the contract around it.
glossary.SCA: Security Configuration Assessment — checking a machine's settings against a hardening benchmark.
glossary.Rules of Engagement: The written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.RoE: Rules of Engagement — the written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.triage: Quickly sorting alerts into real vs noise and deciding what to escalate — like an ER nurse.
glossary.baseline: A record of what 'normal' looks like, so you can spot what's abnormal later.
glossary.chain of custody: A documented trail of who handled each piece of evidence and when — so it holds up as proof.
glossary.agent: A small program installed on each machine that ships its logs to the SOC.
glossary.gate: A checkpoint at the end of a week — finish its required work before the next week unlocks.
glossary.eve.json: The file where Suricata writes its network alerts.
glossary.subnet: A slice of a network sharing an address range, e.g. 10.10.100.x.
glossary.Wazuh: The free, open-source SIEM/SOC platform this lab is built on.
glossary.Suricata: An open-source network intrusion detector that watches traffic and raises alerts.
glossary.Sysmon: A Windows tool that records detailed activity — processes, connections, file changes.
glossary.DVWA: Damn Vulnerable Web App — a deliberately insecure web app used as a safe attack target.
glossary.nmap: A scanner that finds open ports and what software is running on them.
glossary.nikto: A scanner that checks a web server for known issues.
glossary.MITRE ATT&CK: A public catalogue of attacker techniques, used to describe how an attack was carried out.
glossary.MTTD: Mean Time To Detect — the average time from an attack starting to it being noticed.
glossary.MTTR: Mean Time To Respond — the average time from detecting an attack to containing it.
glossary.rule.level: Wazuh scores every alert 0–15 by severity; searching rule.level:>=7 keeps the ones that usually matter.
glossary.rule.groups: The category tags Wazuh puts on an alert (e.g. authentication_failed, ids, web) — handy for filtering by attack type.
glossary.agent.name: The Wazuh field naming which machine an alert came from (e.g. Team07-ubuntu) — use it to filter to one host.
glossary.event channel: A named Windows log stream — Sysmon writes to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational, which the agent forwards.
glossary.Emerging Threats ruleset: The community alert rules Suricata downloads with suricata-update — without them it sees traffic but raises nothing.
glossary.DQL: Dashboard Query Language — the field:value search syntax in the Wazuh/OpenSearch search bar (e.g. data.src_ip:10.10.30.7).
glossary.Discover: The Wazuh/OpenSearch view that lists raw events in a table you can search, add columns to, and save.
glossary.time picker: The date/time control (top-right) that sets which window of events you see — the #1 reason a correct search looks empty.
glossary.visualization: A saved chart (bar, pie, table) built from a search — the building block you drop onto a dashboard.
glossary.dashboard: A saved page of visualizations and searches you assemble to watch at a glance.
glossary.rule.description: The Wazuh field holding the human-readable name of the rule that fired — useful to group and count alerts by.
glossary.syscheck: Wazuh’s File Integrity Monitoring engine; its events carry syscheck.path and whether a file was added/modified/deleted.
glossary.sensor: A program on a machine that watches activity and reports it to the SOC — your Wazuh agent, Suricata and Sysmon are all sensors.
glossary.endpoint: Any individual computer on the network — a laptop, server or VM — as opposed to the network gear between them.
glossary.telemetry: The stream of activity data a machine sends about itself — processes, logins, connections — that the SOC watches.
glossary.hash: A short fingerprint calculated from a file; change one byte and the fingerprint changes, so it proves the file was not tampered with.
glossary.hashing: Running a file through a formula to get its fixed-length fingerprint (its hash).
glossary.SHA-256: A widely trusted hashing method that turns any file into a 64-character fingerprint.
glossary.false positive: An alert that turned out to be harmless — the tool flagged something that was not actually an attack.
glossary.true positive: An alert that was real — the flagged activity really was malicious.
glossary.enroll: To register a machine with the SOC so its agent starts sending logs.
glossary.brute force: Guessing a password by automatically trying huge numbers of combinations until one works.
glossary.port scan: Probing a machine to list which network ports are open, to discover what services it is running.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell — a way to log in to and run commands on another machine over the network, from your terminal.
glossary.pivot: To follow a clue (like an IP or username) from one log into related events, tracing an attacker’s movements.
glossary.hardening: Making a machine harder to attack by closing unused services, fixing weak settings and applying updates.
glossary.containment: Stopping an attack from spreading — e.g. isolating the affected machine — once you have detected it.
glossary.vulnerability: A weakness in software or configuration that an attacker could exploit.
glossary.vuln: Short for vulnerability — a weakness an attacker could exploit.
glossary.firewall: A filter that allows or blocks network connections by rule, to keep unwanted traffic out.
glossary.ufw: Uncomplicated Firewall — the simple command-line firewall on Ubuntu (e.g. ufw allow 22).
glossary.VLAN: A virtual LAN — one physical switch split into separate networks. Ports in different VLANs cannot talk without something routing between them, which is the whole point.
glossary.trunk: A link between switches that carries several VLANs at once, tagging each frame with its VLAN id (802.1Q). The alternative is one cable per VLAN.
glossary.native VLAN: The one VLAN a trunk carries UNTAGGED. If the two ends disagree about which it is, traffic silently lands in the wrong network — the classic trunk fault.
glossary.SVI: Switched Virtual Interface — a VLAN’s gateway configured on the switch itself. A switch with SVIs routes between VLANs at wire speed; a switch without them needs a router.
glossary.router-on-a-stick: Inter-VLAN routing done by a router over a single trunk, with one subinterface per VLAN. What you build when the switch cannot route — same outcome, one link carrying all of it.
glossary.EtherChannel: Two or more physical links bundled into one logical link, so a cable can fail without an outage and the bandwidth adds up. LACP is the protocol that negotiates it.
glossary.spanning tree: The protocol that stops a loop when switches have more than one path between them, by blocking all but one. It always picks a root switch — set it deliberately or it picks the oldest one.
glossary.PortFast: Tells spanning tree an access port has a PC on it, not a switch, so it forwards immediately instead of waiting. Never on a port that could reach another switch.
glossary.BPDU Guard: Shuts a PortFast port the moment it hears spanning-tree messages — which means somebody plugged a switch into a desk port. The protection that makes PortFast safe.
glossary.OSPF: A routing protocol: routers tell each other which networks they can reach, so each works out its own routes. It replaces static routes and reacts when a link dies.
glossary.OSPF area: A grouping that limits how far routing detail spreads. This course uses a single area 0 — the backbone — because one correctly adjacent area is the CCNA outcome.
glossary.adjacency: Two OSPF routers that have agreed to exchange routes. It has to reach the FULL state; anything less is the protocol telling you what does not match.
glossary.NAT: Network Address Translation — rewriting addresses as traffic crosses the edge, so internal addresses that mean nothing on the internet can still reach it.
glossary.PAT: Port Address Translation, sometimes "NAT overload" — the whole company sharing one public address, told apart by port number. What almost every small site actually runs.
glossary.ACL: Access Control List — an ordered list of permit and deny rules applied to an interface in one direction. It ends with an implicit deny, which is why the order matters.
glossary.port security: Limits which or how many MAC addresses a switch port accepts, so a stranger plugging into a desk port cannot quietly join the network.
glossary.ip helper-address: Tells a router to forward DHCP requests from a VLAN to a DHCP server somewhere else. The enterprise pattern, versus the router serving DHCP itself.
glossary.SNMP: The protocol a monitoring system uses to read a device’s interfaces, CPU and memory. Read-only is all a NOC needs; v3 is the version with real authentication.
glossary.syslog: Device log messages sent to a central collector. With synchronised clocks it turns "it broke this morning" into a readable sequence across every device.
glossary.NetBox: The source of truth for the network: sites, devices, interfaces, cables, VLANs and prefixes, with an API. It replaces the spreadsheet once the spreadsheet stops scaling.
glossary.Oxidized: Collects every device’s configuration on a schedule and commits it to Git, so you have both a backup and a history of what changed.
glossary.source of truth: The one system that DEFINES what the network should be. Tools read from it and configure devices to match, so the documentation cannot drift from reality.
glossary.PoE: Power over Ethernet — the switch powering the device on the far end of the cable, which is how phones and access points run without a plug of their own.
glossary.SFP: The slot a fibre (or copper) transceiver plugs into, for uplinks that go further or faster than the built-in ports.

red.blurb: You’re the ethical attacker — you find and prove the weaknesses before a real attacker does.
red.arc: Wk1 recon → Wk2 scan for weaknesses → Wk3 exploit with proof → Wk4 write up findings.
red.handsOffTo: GRC (your findings) and Blue (your attack evidence)
red.waitsOnFrom: GRC (the signed scope that authorizes testing)

blue.blurb: You’re the defender — you harden the systems, watch for the attack, and respond when it happens.
blue.arc: Wk1 harden the hosts → Wk2 set up monitoring → Wk3 detect & contain the attack → Wk4 report the incident.
blue.handsOffTo: GRC (what you hardened and the incident write-up)
blue.waitsOnFrom: GRC (the hardening standard) and Red (the attack to detect)

grc.blurb: You’re governance — you set the rules, score the risk, and turn everyone’s work into the reports.
grc.arc: Wk1 scope & asset inventory → Wk2 risk register → Wk3 policy & response plan → Wk4 final report & briefing.
grc.handsOffTo: Red & Blue (scope, standards) and leadership (the final report)

arch.blurb: Cloud Architect — you set the standards, own the cost and the design, and assemble each week’s document.
arch.arc: Standards & budget → architecture & cost → access & network design → IaC map → handover.
arch.handsOffTo: the whole team (the standard every resource follows)
arch.waitsOnFrom: nobody to start — each role fills its own section

infra.blurb: Infrastructure Admin — you build the network, the VM, the data store and, later, the template.
infra.arc: Network → VM → database → alerts → subnets & disks → snapshots → IaC → rebuild from the template.
infra.handsOffTo: App & DevOps (the resources they deploy onto)
infra.waitsOnFrom: nobody to start — your task stands alone each week

dev.blurb: App & DevOps — you ship the website, the serverless API and the pipeline that deploys them.
dev.arc: Repo → website → API → debugging → identity → patching → restores → deploy from code → CI/CD.
dev.handsOffTo: Security & Ops (the endpoints to lock down)
dev.waitsOnFrom: nobody to start — your task stands alone each week

secops.blurb: Security & Ops — you lock access down, prove what must fail does fail, and work the incidents.
secops.arc: Firewall → SSH from your IP → CORS → incident → denials → no open ports → drills → OIDC → posture.
secops.waitsOnFrom: nobody to start — your task stands alone each week
